entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III)

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 11 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits (Part I)

This post continues the problem of two fixed centres from part 4 and part 6.

New types of orbits

At the end of part 6 I wrote:

The moving body never crosses the saddle point of the potential between the two centres, so it stays around only one of the fixed masses. This disagrees with the theory: \(S\) should behave like \(\operatorname{sn}\), so \(\sigma\) should sweep through its whole range. […] A larger initial velocity may let it pass the saddle point.

That guess was right: the assumption of zero initial velocity was too restrictive. Carefully varying the initial velocity produces two new types of orbit, lemniscate and planetary.

To classify them, we need two constants of motion. With the centres at \((\pm d, 0)\) and masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\),

\[\begin{aligned} G&=\frac{1}{2}\left(x p_y-y p_x\right)^2+\frac{1}{2} d^2 p_x^2+d x\left(\frac{m_1}{\sqrt{(x+d)^2+y^2}}-\frac{m_2}{\sqrt{(x-d)^2+y^2}}\right), \\ H&=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_x^2+p_y^2\right)-\frac{m_1}{\sqrt{(x+d)^2+y^2}}-\frac{m_2}{\sqrt{(x-d)^2+y^2}} . \end{aligned}\]

\(H\) is the Hamiltonian (the energy), and \(G\) is the additional constant of motion discovered by Euler, which makes the problem integrable.

The paper Syzygies in the Two Center Problem shows that the values of \(H\) and \(G\) determine the type of orbit: \(S\) (satellite, the type we found earlier), \(L\) (lemniscate) and \(P\) (planetary).

My simulations reproduce all three types:

With these orbits, \(S\) now covers its full range. However, it still looks rather irregular and does not yet clearly follow \(\operatorname{sn}\):

I also computed the parameter \(e\) from Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics, where \(e>1\) and \(e<1\) correspond to different types of orbit. The lemniscate orbit has a much larger value, around \(e \approx 2.5\); the satellite orbit has the smallest, around \(e \approx 0.98\); and the planetary orbit has \(e \approx 1.08\). Understanding this is the next step.

Future work

  • Map out which initial conditions lead to each of \(S\), \(L\) and \(P\), in the hope of finding new types of orbit.
  • Extend the analysis to unequal fixed masses.
  • Check whether the mass of the test particle matters.

Progress

Progress has been faster than I expected. With three weeks of the project left, it is time to start drafting the final report and poster, which keeping this log up to date makes much easier. Making a genuinely original contribution in the remaining time is ambitious, but I will see how far I can get.

Credits

This post draws on Syzygies in the Two Center Problem and the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. Nothing in the results.

What changed. The set-up now gives the positions of the two fixed masses, and the eccentricities read off the plots are marked as approximate.
entry.summary: Two constants of motion classify the orbits of the two-centre problem into satellite, lemniscate and planetary types, all reproduced in simulation.

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 10 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere  ·  Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III) →

This post describes a first systematic search for interesting orbits: a scan over a family of initial conditions, recording which ones stay bounded.

Set-up

My code integrates the motion of three bodies from given initial conditions, and, as we have seen, the trajectories are highly sensitive to those conditions. So let’s scan a family of initial conditions systematically.

Take three unit masses, \(m_1 = m_2 = m_3 = 1\), and \(G=1\). Start them on a line with zero total momentum:

Body Initial position Initial velocity
1 \((-1, 0)\) \((a, b)\)
2 \((1, 0)\) \((a, b)\)
3 \((0, 0)\) \((-2a, -2b)\)

This is the standard family that contains the figure-eight orbit, at about \((a,b) = (0.347, 0.533)\).

I vary \(a\) and \(b\) independently from \(0\) to \(1\) in steps of \(0.01\). Each simulation runs for \(50\,000\) steps with \(\Delta t = 0.001\). If any body moves further than a fixed distance from the origin before the end, the run returns False (escaped); otherwise it returns True and the point \((a, b)\) is plotted. Many initial conditions lead to escapes or near-collisions, and a few lead to periodic orbits.

Results

Around the figure-eight orbit, the outcome is more sensitive to changes in the vertical velocity \(b\) than to changes in \(a\). This agrees with the findings of an earlier Edinburgh vacation-project report by F. Ramos.

A finer scan of that region (about 15 hours):

Limitations

The escape radius I used, \(20\), turned out to be too generous: many runs counted as “bounded” are not periodic in any useful sense.

Choosing the radius is genuinely difficult, because the three-body problem has no natural bound on the separations. In the two-body problem, negative energy forces a bounded orbit. With three bodies, two of them can form a tight binary whose potential energy is arbitrarily negative, which leaves the third body enough energy to travel arbitrarily far, and possibly return, while the total energy stays negative. With unit masses and \(G = 1\), the potential energy is

\[V = -\left(\frac{1}{r_{12}} + \frac{1}{r_{23}} + \frac{1}{r_{13}}\right),\]

and making one separation small makes \(V\) as negative as we like, whatever the other two separations are. So there is no cut-off that cleanly separates “bound” from “escaping”.

A better criterion: the return proximity function

A more targeted test looks for orbits that come back close to where they started in phase space, using the return proximity function

\[P(t)=\left|\mathbf{X}(t)-\mathbf{X}_0\right|=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^3\left[\mathbf{r}_i(t)-\mathbf{r}_i(0)\right]^2+\sum_{i=1}^3\left[\mathbf{p}_i(t) - \mathbf{p}_i(0)\right]^2} .\]

For a periodic orbit, \(P(t)\) oscillates and dips close to zero once per period: the smaller the minimum, the closer the orbit returns to its initial state. In the next run I will keep orbits with \(P<15\) throughout the simulation and \(\min_{t > 0} P(t) < 0.7\).

Progress

Each scan takes over 30 hours. The code is already fairly optimised, so the next step is to check whether a larger time step (\(0.01\) instead of \(0.001\)) keeps enough accuracy. Five of the eight weeks have passed, and the search for genuinely new orbits is the most open-ended part of the project.

Credits

This search is inspired by the paper New Families of Periodic Orbits for the Planar Three-Body Problem Computed with High Precision.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong.

  • The initial conditions put the body with velocity \(-2(a, b)\) at \((1, 0)\). The figure-eight values quoted, \((a, b) \approx (0.35, 0.53)\), belong to the standard arrangement with that body at the origin, which the table now gives.
  • The potential energy was written \(1/a + 1/b + 1/c\). Gravitational potential energy is negative: \(V = -(1/r_{12} + 1/r_{23} + 1/r_{13})\).
  • The argument for why no cut-off radius works did not hold up. The real reason is that two bodies can form a tight binary with arbitrarily negative potential energy, which leaves the third body enough energy to travel arbitrarily far.
  • The return proximity function compared the momenta with zero instead of with their initial values.

What changed. All are fixed, and the diary-style asides are shorter.
entry.summary: A brute-force scan of initial velocities for three equal masses: which starting conditions stay bounded, where the figure eight sits, and how to search better.

entry.title: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere

link.title: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 9 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)  ·  Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits (Part I) →

This post outlines the proof that the figure-eight orbit exists, following Chenciner and Montgomery. It uses the shape sphere together with the direct method of the calculus of variations.

Outline of the proof

  1. On the shape sphere, minimise the action over paths that start at an Euler configuration (three bodies collinear, one at the midpoint of the other two) and end at an isosceles configuration. The minimiser is one twelfth of the orbit.
  2. Show that the minimiser has no collisions. Let \(A_2\) be a lower bound for the action of any path with a collision, and exhibit a collision-free test path whose action is smaller than \(A_2\). Then the minimiser cannot collide.
  3. Use the symmetries of the equal-mass problem to make twelve copies of this arc, and show that they join smoothly into one closed curve on the shape sphere.
  4. Reconstruct the motion in the plane from the curve on the shape sphere, and show that the three bodies follow a single figure-eight-shaped curve.

The figure eight is special: numerical work by Simó indicates that it is stable, which is very rare among choreographies (orbits in which all the bodies follow the same curve). By contrast, Lagrange’s equilateral circular orbit with three equal masses is a choreography too, but it is unstable (see Routh’s criterion in part 8).

Step 1: finding minimisers

The action

Following Chenciner and Montgomery, define the action

\[A = \int_{0}^{T} \left(\tfrac{1}{2}K+U\right) dt ,\]

where \(K = \lvert\dot x\rvert^2\) is twice the kinetic energy and \(U\) is the force function (the negative of the potential energy). The action is minimised over the set \(\Lambda\) of paths in the Sobolev space \(H^1([0,T], X)\) that start at an Euler configuration (of arbitrary size) and end at an isosceles configuration. Here

\[X = \left\{ x=(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{C}^3 \;\middle|\; \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i =0 \right\},\]

and \(H^1\) consists of paths that, together with their time derivatives, are square integrable, which is the right setting for the direct method.

Step 2: the minimiser has no collisions

Collisions are expensive

If a path in \(\Lambda\) has a collision (double or triple), its action is at least \(A_2\), where \(A_2\) is the action of the collinear two-body solution in which two unit masses start at collision and come to rest a time \(T\) later, with the centre of mass fixed.

A cheaper test path

The Euler equipotential length satisfies \(\ell_0< \pi/5\). Using this bound, one constructs an explicit collision-free test path, running along an equipotential curve on the shape sphere, whose action \(a\) is smaller than \(A_2\).

Conclusion

Putting these together,

\[\min_{\Lambda} A \;\le\; a \;<\; A_2 \;\le\; A(\text{any path with a collision}),\]

so the minimiser is collision-free.

Step 3: assembling the full orbit

The main difficulty is to show that the copies fit together smoothly at their endpoints.

The first task is to show that the minimising arc meets the two curves \(E_3\) and \(M_1\) that constrain its endpoints at right angles. Recall the first variation of the action:

\[\delta A = \epsilon \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\, \eta \right]_0^T + \epsilon \int_0^T \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right) \eta \, dt .\]

Usually the boundary term vanishes because the endpoints are fixed, so \(\eta(0)=\eta(T)=0\). Here the endpoints may slide along \(E_3\) and \(M_1\), so \(\eta\) need not vanish there. The integral vanishes because the minimiser satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, so we need

\[\left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right|_{t=0} \cdot \eta(0) = 0, \qquad \left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right|_{t=T} \cdot \eta(T) = 0\]

for every allowed \(\eta\). Since \(\partial L/\partial \dot{x}\) points along the minimising curve, and \(\eta\) can be any vector tangent to the constraint curves, the minimising arc must meet \(E_3\) and \(M_1\) orthogonally. Reflecting across these curves then extends the arc smoothly.

Step 4: from the shape sphere back to the plane

Periodicity

Suppose the curve on the shape sphere is closed. Then the initial and final triangles in the plane are similar, because they correspond to the same point of the shape sphere. What is the angle of rotation between them?

For motions with zero angular momentum, the area rule answers this: the rotation angle equals twice the spherical area enclosed by the shape curve (on the shape sphere of radius \(\tfrac12\), as normalised by Chenciner and Montgomery).

The figure below defines the points \(E_i\) on the equator (the collinear configurations with body \(i\) in the middle) and the meridian \(M_1\):

Combining the area rule with the symmetries shows that the three bodies move along the same curve and differ only by a phase:

No extra loops

Finally, one shows that the angular momentum of each individual body about the centre of mass vanishes only when that body passes through the origin. So each body’s polar angle changes monotonically on each lobe, and each lobe is star-shaped: the curve has no extra loops. The curve traced out is therefore a figure eight.

Progress

This has been a long and intense stretch of the project, but I am well ahead of my original plan.

Credits

This proof is not original. It follows A. Chenciner and R. Montgomery, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses, Annals of Mathematics 152 (2000), 881–901, and the presentation I’ve Got a Three-Body Problem by Gareth E. Roberts (College of the Holy Cross).

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. The outline stated the key step the wrong way round. It said to show that every collision-free path has a smaller action than the cheapest path with a collision. What the proof needs is one collision-free test path whose action is below a lower bound for all paths with collisions; then the minimiser cannot collide.

What changed. The outline is rewritten in numbered steps, the configuration space is written \(X\) instead of \(\chi\), and the variational argument at the end is tidied. Previously titled “A Proof of the Existence of the Figure-8 Orbit using Actions and the Shape Sphere”.
entry.summary: An outline of Chenciner and Montgomery's variational proof: minimise the action over one twelfth of the orbit, rule out collisions, and assemble the figure eight.

entry.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)

link.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 8 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)  ·  Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere →

Continuing from part 7, this post estimates how many terms of Sundman’s series are needed in a simple example, and shows why the series is useless in practice.

Lagrange’s equilateral solution

In 1772 Lagrange found a family of solutions in which the three bodies form an equilateral triangle at every instant. In the restricted problem, the small body then sits at one of the \(L_4\) or \(L_5\) Lagrange points, also called Trojan points.

The configuration is linearly stable only when one mass dominates. In the restricted problem, the two large masses must differ by a factor of more than about \(25\) (Routh’s criterion: a mass ratio above \(24.96\)). Otherwise any small perturbation grows and the triangle breaks up:

Estimating the number of terms

In the unperturbed solution each body moves on a circle, which we parametrise as \((x,y) = (\cos t, \sin t)\).

The mutual distances stay constant, say equal to \(r\), so Sundman’s factor

\[\Gamma = \left(1-e^{-r/l}\right)^3\]

is constant too, and \(t=\Gamma w\). Using the map from the previous post,

\[t=\frac{2 \Omega \Gamma}{\pi} \log \frac{1+\tau}{1-\tau} = 2A\left(\tau + \frac{\tau^3}{3} + \frac{\tau^5}{5}+ O(\tau^7)\right), \qquad A = \frac{2\Omega\Gamma}{\pi} .\]

Substituting into the Taylor series of \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) gives the coordinates as power series in \(\tau\):

\[\begin{aligned} \cos t &= 1 - 2A^2 \tau^2 - \left(\tfrac{4}{3} A^2 - \tfrac{2}{3} A^4\right) \tau^4 - \left(\tfrac{46}{45}A^2 - \tfrac{8}{9} A^4 + \tfrac{4}{45} A^6\right) \tau^6+O(\tau^8), \\ \sin t &= 2A \tau + \left(\tfrac{2}{3}A - \tfrac{4}{3} A^3\right) \tau^3 + \left(\tfrac{2}{5}A - \tfrac{4}{3}A^3 + \tfrac{4}{15} A^5\right) \tau^5 + O(\tau^7) . \end{aligned}\]

Now take masses \((m_0, m_1, m_2) = \left(\tfrac{1}{200}, \tfrac{1}{200}, \tfrac{99}{100}\right)\). For this configuration \(\Omega < 9 \times 10^{-8}\), which gives \(A < 4 \times 10^{-8}\).

How many terms do we need to follow the motion up to \(t = 1\)? Truncating the series for \(t\) after \(n\) terms, to get within \(0.1\) of \(t = 1\) we need

\[2A \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\tau^{2k-1}}{2k-1} > 0.9, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad S_\tau := \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\tau^{2k-1}}{2k-1} > \frac{9}{20A} .\]

With \(A< 4 \times 10^{-8}\) this requires \(S_\tau > 10^7\).

Compare with the partial sums of the odd harmonic series,

\[S_p=\sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{1}{2k-1} \approx \tfrac12 \ln p + \text{const}.\]

Reaching \(S_p > S\) requires \(p>e^{2S-2.4}\), so \(S_p > 10^7\) requires \(p > 10^{8 \times 10^{6}}\). Since \(\lvert\tau\rvert < 1\), each term of \(S_\tau\) is smaller than the corresponding term of \(S_p\), so \(S_\tau\) needs at least as many terms: \(n > p > 10^{8 \times 10^{6}}\).

So even in this simple, collision-free example, about \(10^{8\,000\,000}\) terms are needed for one decimal place of accuracy. Sundman’s series converges, but far too slowly ever to be used.

Progress

The coding side of the project is now essentially complete, so I can concentrate on the theory, which will also form the core of my final report. Things have gone more smoothly than I expected.

Credits

This post is based on D. K. Yeomans’s exposition of Sundman’s work and on Belorizky’s paper (1930).

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong.

  • In the series for \(\cos t\), the coefficient \(\tfrac{46}{45}\) was written \(\tfrac{45}{46}\).
  • The factor \(\Gamma\) was written with \(e^{1/l}\) instead of \(e^{-r/l}\).
  • The sum \(\sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{1}{2k-1}\) had \(2p-1\) in the denominator, and the error term after \(\tau^5\) is \(O(\tau^7)\), not \(O(\tau^6)\).
  • A reference link no longer worked.

What changed. All are fixed, and the estimate of the number of terms is explained step by step.
entry.summary: Applying Sundman's series to Lagrange's equilateral solution shows why it is impractical: it needs more than 10 to the power 8 million terms for one digit of accuracy.

entry.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)

link.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 7 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)  ·  Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II) →

In 1912 Karl F. Sundman found a convergent power-series solution to the three-body problem, valid whenever the total angular momentum is non-zero. In principle this is a general solution, but its convergence is so slow that it is of no practical use. This post outlines how it works.

Key points of Sundman’s paper

  • At a double (binary) collision, the distance to the third, non-colliding body stays bounded.
  • A triple collision can only occur if the total angular momentum (the “area integral”) is zero.
  • At a double collision, the velocities and accelerations of the colliding bodies tend to infinity.
  • The unit vector along the line joining the two colliding bodies tends to a limit.
  • The singularity of a collision between a given pair of bodies can be removed by introducing a new independent variable \(u\).
  • A different independent variable \(w\) removes all the double-collision singularities at once, allowing any number and combination of double collisions.
  • The coordinates of the three bodies can then be expanded as power series in \(w\).
  • These series converge for all time, although extremely slowly.

The regularising variable \(w\)

Where the singularities come from

The variable \(u\) regularises a collision between one particular pair of bodies, say \(m_0\) and \(m_1\). The equations of motion contain terms such as \(1/r_0\) and \(1/r_1\), where the \(r_i\) are mutual distances, so a collision involving a different pair still produces a singularity. We need a variable that treats all three pairs symmetrically.

Definition

Sundman’s variable \(w\) is defined by

\[dt= \Gamma\, dw, \qquad w=0 \text{ at } t=0,\]

where

\[\Gamma = \left(1-e^{-r_0/l}\right)\left(1-e^{-r_1/l}\right)\left(1-e^{-r_2/l}\right)\]

for a suitable constant \(l\), and \(r_0, r_1, r_2\) are the three mutual distances. The definition is symmetric in the three distances, so every double collision is regularised in the same way.

Convergence in a strip

After a long analysis (Yeomans gives a complete account), one finds that the coordinates are holomorphic functions of \(w\) in a strip around the real axis,

\[\lvert \operatorname{Im} w\rvert < \Omega,\]

for some \(\Omega > 0\): a strip of width \(2\Omega\).

Mapping the strip to a disc

A power series converges in a disc, not a strip, so we map the strip conformally onto the unit disc.

Write the strip as \(S = \{s : \lvert\operatorname{Im} s\rvert < \beta\}\). The exponential map

\[g(s) = e^{\pi s / (2\beta)}\]

sends \(S\) onto the right half-plane \(\{\operatorname{Re} z > 0\}\). Points of the right half-plane are closer to \(1\) than to \(-1\), i.e. \(\lvert z-1\rvert < \lvert z+1\rvert\), so the Möbius transformation

\[h(z)=\frac{z-1}{z+1}\]

maps the right half-plane onto the unit disc. The composition \(h \circ g\) therefore maps \(S\) onto the unit disc. With \(\beta = \Omega\), the new variable \(\tau = h(g(w))\) satisfies

\[w = \frac{2 \Omega}{\pi} \log\frac{1+ \tau}{1- \tau},\]

and the coordinates become power series in \(\tau\) that converge for \(\lvert\tau\rvert < 1\). The whole real time axis, \(-\infty < w < \infty\), corresponds to the real interval \(-1 < \tau < 1\) (a good exercise to check).

This is also the source of the slow convergence: late times are squeezed towards the boundary \(\lvert\tau\rvert = 1\) of the disc of convergence, where power series converge very slowly.

When does it work?

The series exist whenever the total angular momentum is non-zero,

\[\mathbf{c} = m_0 (\mathbf{r}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_0) + m_1 (\mathbf{r}_1\times \mathbf{v}_1) + m_2 ( \mathbf{r}_2 \times \mathbf{v}_2) \neq \mathbf{0} .\]

That covers essentially every case, including double collisions, but not triple collisions, which require \(\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}\).

The catch is the convergence rate: Belorizky estimated that something like \(10^{8\,000\,000}\) terms would be needed for useful accuracy in a simple case. Part 8 goes through the estimate.

Summary

Sundman found an independent variable \(w\) in which every double collision is regular. The solution is analytic in a strip of width \(2\Omega\) around the real \(w\)-axis, which a conformal map sends to the unit disc in a new variable \(\tau\). The resulting power series in \(\tau\) solve the three-body problem for all time whenever the angular momentum is non-zero, but they converge far too slowly to be useful.

Progress

Alongside the reading, I have been simulating the Broucke–Hadjidemetriou–Hénon (BHH) orbits. Here is one, with its curve on the shape sphere seen from two angles:

Credits

This post is based on D. K. Yeomans’s exposition of Sundman’s regularisation of the three-body problem, NASA technical memorandum X-640-66-481 (1966), and on notes by Peter Senchyna.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong.

  • The map from the right half-plane to the unit disc was written \(h(z) = \lvert z-1\rvert / \lvert z+1\rvert\), which is a number, not a map. It is the Möbius transformation \(h(z) = (z-1)/(z+1)\).
  • The strip was written \(\operatorname{Im} s \le \beta\) instead of \(\lvert\operatorname{Im} s\rvert < \beta\), and the condition on \(w\) used \(\lvert w - \bar w\rvert\), which is twice \(\lvert\operatorname{Im} w\rvert\).
  • A reference link no longer worked.

What changed. All are fixed, and the reference now points to the copy on NASA’s Technical Reports Server.
entry.summary: Sundman's 1912 series solves the three-body problem for non-zero angular momentum. How the regularising variable works, and why the series is useless in practice.

entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 6 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere  ·  Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I) →

This post continues the problem of two fixed centres, introduced in part 4, by converting my simulated trajectories into the coordinates in which the theory is written.

From Cartesian to prolate spheroidal coordinates

Recall the prolate spheroidal coordinates \((R, \sigma)\), with the centres at distance \(b\) from the origin and \(\sigma \in [0, \pi]\):

\[x= \pm \sqrt{R^2-b^2}\, \sin \sigma, \qquad z=R \cos \sigma .\]

The sign of \(x\) is carried by the \(\pm\), so it is enough to consider \(x \geq 0\). Take \(b = 1\).

Substituting \(R = z/\cos\sigma\) into the first equation and squaring,

\[\begin{aligned} x^2 &= \sin^2 \sigma \left(\frac{z^2}{\cos^2 \sigma} - 1\right) = \frac{(z^2 - \cos^2 \sigma)\sin^2 \sigma}{\cos^2 \sigma} \\ &= \frac{(z^2 - 1 + \sin^2 \sigma)\sin^2 \sigma}{1 - \sin^2 \sigma}, \end{aligned}\]

which rearranges to

\[x^2 = \sin^2 \sigma \left(x^2 + z^2 - 1 + \sin^2 \sigma\right).\]

(This step divides by \(\cos\sigma\), so it fails on the line \(z = 0\), which has to be handled separately.) Setting \(u=\sin^2\sigma\) gives a quadratic,

\[u^2+(x^2+z^2-1)\,u-x^2=0,\]

whose non-negative root is

\[u = \frac{-(x^2 + z^2 - 1) + \sqrt{(x^2 + z^2 - 1)^2 + 4x^2}}{2} .\]

Then \(\sigma_1 = \arcsin\sqrt{u}\) lies in \([0, \pi/2]\). Since \(z = R\cos\sigma\) with \(R \ge 0\), this is the correct angle when \(z \ge 0\); when \(z<0\) the angle lies in \((\pi/2, \pi]\), and we take \(\sigma = \pi - \sigma_1\):

\[\sigma = \begin{cases} \sigma_1, & z \ge 0, \\ \pi - \sigma_1, & z < 0. \end{cases}\]

Given \(\sigma\), \(R = z/\cos\sigma\) follows immediately (or \(R = \sqrt{x^2/\sin^2\sigma + b^2}\) near \(z = 0\)).

Results

For this trajectory:

the coordinate \(R\) evolves as

the angle \(\sigma\) as

and \(S = \cos\sigma\) as

Issues

The moving body never crosses the saddle point of the potential between the two centres (analogous to a Lagrange point), so it stays around only one of the fixed masses. This disagrees with the theory: \(S\) should behave like the Jacobi function \(\operatorname{sn}\), so \(\sigma\) should sweep through its whole range, whereas here it covers only part of it.

Two assumptions may be responsible:

  • I implemented the fixed centres by holding two bodies in place; it may be better to give them very large masses instead.
  • The test body starts at rest. A larger initial velocity may let it pass the saddle point.

Progress

Matching the constants in the book to the parameters in my code has been the hardest part so far. Over the next weeks I plan to study Sundman’s series, which I expect to be computationally very demanding.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. The discussion of which branch of \(\arcsin\) to take described \(\sigma\) in the range \(\pi/2 < \sigma < 3\pi/2\), but in these coordinates \(\sigma\) only runs from 0 to \(\pi\).

What changed. The rule is now stated directly: \(\sigma = \sigma_1\) when \(z \ge 0\) and \(\sigma = \pi - \sigma_1\) when \(z < 0\).
entry.summary: Converting simulated trajectories from Cartesian to prolate spheroidal coordinates, and why the first results disagreed with the theory.

entry.title: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere

link.title: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 5 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)  ·  Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II) →

This post introduces the shape sphere, a way to picture the motion of three bodies by keeping track only of the shape of the triangle they form.

Reducing the three-body problem

Reduction simplifies the three-body problem by removing degrees of freedom associated with symmetries.

Let the three bodies lie in the plane, identified with \(\mathbb{C}\). Before reduction, the configuration space is \(\mathbb{C}^3\), the positions of the three masses. By Galilean invariance we can fix the centre of mass at the origin, which reduces the configuration space to

\[X = \left\{ x = (x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{C}^3 \;\middle|\; \sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 0 \right\} \cong \mathbb{C}^2 .\]

Next come the rotations and reflections of the plane, which act by

\[R_\theta \cdot (x_1, x_2, x_3) = (e^{i\theta} x_1, e^{i\theta} x_2, e^{i\theta} x_3), \qquad S \cdot (x_1, x_2, x_3) = (\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2, \bar{x}_3).\]

Taking the quotient of \(X\) by the rotation group \(SO(2)\) gives a space homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), whose points are oriented congruence classes of triangles. Fixing the overall size as well, by setting the moment of inertia to \(I = 1\), leaves a 2-sphere whose points are oriented similarity classes of triangles: the shape sphere.

The maps

For equal masses, the Jacobi map \(\mathcal{J}: X \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^2\) is

\[\left(z_1, z_2\right)=\mathcal{J}\left(x_1, x_2, x_3\right)=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(x_3-x_2\right),\ \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left(x_1-\frac{1}{2}\left(x_2+x_3\right)\right)\right),\]

and the Hopf map \(\mathcal{K}: \mathbb{C}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}^3\) is

\[\mathcal{K}\left(z_1, z_2\right)=\left(u_1,\ u_2+i u_3\right)=\left(\left|z_1\right|^2-\left|z_2\right|^2,\ 2 \bar{z}_1 z_2\right) .\]

One checks that

\[\left|\mathcal{K}\left(z_1, z_2\right)\right|^2=u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=\left(\left|z_1\right|^2+\left|z_2\right|^2\right)^2=I^2,\]

where \(I = \lvert z_1\rvert^2 + \lvert z_2\rvert^2\) is the moment of inertia. So \(\mathcal{K} \circ \mathcal{J}\) sends the 3-sphere \(I = 1\) onto the unit 2-sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), and rotating the triangle (multiplying \((z_1, z_2)\) by \(e^{i\theta}\)) does not change the image. This is the Hopf fibration. The details are in Chenciner and Montgomery’s paper, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses.

Plotting in Python

Here is the figure-eight orbit traced on the shape sphere:

The same picture works for other periodic orbits; the Three-body gallery is a good place to explore them.

Progress

Working out how to plot the shape sphere, and reading the underlying theory, took several days. Long calculations can obscure the intuition, which is exactly what pictures like these help to restore. Next I return to the problem of two fixed centres, to classify the orbits of a body attracted by them.

Credits

This post is based on A. Chenciner and R. Montgomery, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses, Annals of Mathematics 152 (2000), 881–901.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. Nothing in the content.

What changed. The reduction is explained more clearly, the notation is consistent, and there is a link to Chenciner and Montgomery’s paper.
entry.summary: Reducing the planar three-body problem by translations, rotations and scaling: the Jacobi map, the Hopf map, and orbits drawn on the shape sphere.

entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)

entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 4 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem  ·  Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere →

This post introduces the problem of two fixed centres, also known as Euler’s three-body problem: a small body moving under the gravity of two masses held fixed in place. Unlike the general three-body problem, it is integrable.

Momentum conservation fixed

In part 2 I noted that the total momentum in my simulation was drifting. The cause turned out to be a bug: an accumulator for the momentum components was not reset to zero at each time step. With the fix, the remaining error is at the level of floating-point round-off, about \(10^{-15}\):

Set-up

The two fixed masses \(m_\pm\) sit on the \(z\)-axis at \(z = \pm b\), and the third body moves in the \(x\)–\(z\) plane.

Simulation

To simulate the problem, I held two of the masses fixed and let the third move freely:

The Lagrangian

The natural coordinates are prolate spheroidal coordinates \((R, \sigma)\), which play the role of polar coordinates but with two foci:

\[x = \pm \sqrt{R^2-b^2}\, \sin \sigma, \qquad z = R \cos \sigma .\]

Writing \(\mathbf{r}(R, \sigma) = (x, z)\), the partial derivatives are

\[\frac{\partial x}{\partial R} = \pm \frac{R \sin \sigma}{\sqrt{R^2 - b^2}}, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial R} = \cos \sigma, \qquad \frac{\partial x}{\partial \sigma} = \pm \sqrt{R^2 - b^2}\, \cos \sigma, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial \sigma} = -R \sin \sigma,\]

so (taking the \(+\) sign)

\[\mathbf{r}_R = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial R} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{R \sin \sigma}{\sqrt{R^2 - b^2}} \\ \cos \sigma \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{r}_\sigma = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{R^2 - b^2}\, \cos \sigma \\ -R \sin \sigma \end{pmatrix} .\]

The metric components \(g_{RR}= \mathbf{r}_R \cdot \mathbf{r}_R\), \(g_{R\sigma} = \mathbf{r}_R\cdot\mathbf{r}_\sigma\) and \(g_{\sigma\sigma} = \mathbf{r}_\sigma\cdot\mathbf{r}_\sigma\) come out as

\[g_{RR}=\frac{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}{R^2-b^2}, \qquad g_{R \sigma}=0, \qquad g_{\sigma \sigma}=R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma .\]

The distances to the two centres are \(R \mp b\cos\sigma\), so the potential energy per unit mass is

\[V=-\mu\, \frac{R+\beta b \cos \sigma}{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}, \qquad \mu = G(m_+ + m_-), \qquad \beta=\frac{m_{+}-m_{-}}{m_{+}+m_{-}} .\]

The Lagrangian per unit mass is therefore

\[\mathcal{L} = T-V =\frac{1}{2}\, \frac{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}{R^2-b^2}\, \dot{R}^2+\frac{1}{2}\left(R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma\right) \dot{\sigma}^2+\mu\, \frac{R+\beta b \cos \sigma}{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma} .\]

Jacobi elliptic functions

The equations of motion separate in these coordinates. Following the book, the angular motion reduces (after a change of independent variable) to an equation of the form

\[S^{\prime 2}=\left(1-S^2\right)\left(1-k^2 S^2\right),\]

whose solution is

\[S=\operatorname{sn}(f+\omega \mid k).\]

Here \(\operatorname{sn}\) is one of the Jacobi elliptic functions. Trigonometric functions are defined with reference to a circle, and the Jacobi elliptic functions generalise them to other conic sections, in particular the ellipse.

To verify the solution, use

\[\frac{d}{du} \operatorname{sn}(u \mid k) = \operatorname{cn}(u \mid k) \operatorname{dn}(u \mid k)\]

together with the identities

\[\operatorname{sn}^2(u \mid k) + \operatorname{cn}^2(u \mid k) = 1, \qquad \operatorname{dn}^2(u \mid k) + k^2 \operatorname{sn}^2(u \mid k) = 1 .\]

With \(u = f + \omega\), these give \(\operatorname{cn}^2 u = 1 - S^2\) and \(\operatorname{dn}^2 u = 1 - k^2 S^2\), so

\[S'^2 = \operatorname{cn}^2(u \mid k)\, \operatorname{dn}^2(u \mid k) = (1 - S^2)(1 - k^2 S^2) .\]

Progress

At the end of the first week, the simulation code is in good shape, ahead of my plan, and I have started thinking about the structure of the final report.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna. Parts of the material on Jacobi elliptic functions are from Wikipedia.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. Nothing in the results.

What changed. The Jacobi elliptic function identities behind the last step are shown, the modulus is written \(k\) instead of \(k_{01}\), and the coordinates are introduced more carefully.
entry.summary: Euler's three-body problem: a test mass attracted by two fixed masses. Prolate spheroidal coordinates, the Lagrangian, and Jacobi elliptic functions.

entry.title: Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem
entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 3 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Symplectic Integrators  ·  Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I) →

Before tackling three bodies, this post revisits ellipses and the Kepler problem.

Ellipses

Semi-major and semi-minor axes

I discussed the parametrisation of ellipses in an earlier post. An ellipse can be written as

\[\frac{X^2}{a^2}+\frac{Y^2}{b^2}=1,\]

with semi-major axis \(a\), semi-minor axis \(b\) and eccentricity \(e\), where

\[b^2=a^2(1-e^2).\]

Polar equations

Measured from the centre, at polar angle \(\theta_{\text{c}}\), the radius is

\[R= \frac{a \sqrt{1-e^2}}{\left(1-e^2 \cos^2\theta_{\text{c}}\right)^{1/2}} .\]

Measured from a focus, at polar angle \(\theta_{\text{f}}\), it is

\[r=\frac{a(1-e^2)}{1+e \cos\theta_{\text{f}}} = \frac{p}{1+e \cos\theta_{\text{f}}},\]

where \(p\) is the semi-latus rectum, which appeared in my post on Kepler’s third law.

The two-body problem

I have written about the reduction to relative motion and about two bodies falling straight towards each other. Here I focus on the shape of the orbits. Throughout, \(\mu = GM\) and \(\mathbf{r}\) is the relative position, which obeys \(\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = -\mu\,\mathbf{r}/r^3\).

Energy

The energy per unit (reduced) mass is conserved:

\[\frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{\mu}{r} = E .\]

Suppose \(E<0\) and write \(E=- \alpha^2\). Since \(\frac12 v^2 \ge 0\),

\[\frac{\mu}{r} \ge \alpha^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r \leq \frac{\mu}{\alpha^2} = 2a, \qquad \text{where } a=\frac{\mu}{2 \alpha^2}.\]

So negative energy implies a bounded orbit. (In fact \(a\) turns out to be the semi-major axis.)

Angular momentum and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector

As shown in my post on Noether’s theorem, the angular momentum per unit mass, \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{r}\times\dot{\mathbf{r}}\), is conserved.

If \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{0}\), the motion is purely radial: the bodies move along a straight line, and collide if they are approaching. If \(\mathbf{C} \neq \mathbf{0}\), then \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{C}=0\), so the motion lies in the fixed plane perpendicular to \(\mathbf{C}\).

Next, differentiate the unit vector \(\mathbf{e}_r = \mathbf{r}/r\):

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{d\mathbf{e}_r}{dt}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{r}\right) & =\frac{r \dot{\mathbf{r}}-\dot{r}\, \mathbf{r}}{r^2}=\frac{r^2 \dot{\mathbf{r}}-r \dot{r}\, \mathbf{r}}{r^3} \\ & =\frac{(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \dot{\mathbf{r}}-(\mathbf{r} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{r}}) \mathbf{r}}{r^3}=\frac{\mathbf{r} \times(\dot{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{r})}{r^3}=\frac{\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{r}}{r^3}, \end{aligned}\]

using \(r\dot r = \mathbf{r}\cdot\dot{\mathbf{r}}\) and \(\dot{\mathbf{r}}\times\mathbf{r} = -\mathbf{C}\). Using the equation of motion, \(\mathbf{r}/r^3 = -\ddot{\mathbf{r}}/\mu\), and since \(\mathbf{C}\) is constant,

\[\frac{d\mathbf{e}_r}{dt}=-\frac{\mathbf{C} \times \ddot{\mathbf{r}}}{\mu}=-\frac{1}{\mu} \frac{d}{d t}(\mathbf{C} \times \dot{\mathbf{r}})=\frac{1}{\mu} \frac{d}{d t}(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{C}) .\]

Integrating, there is a constant vector \(\mathbf{e}\) such that

\[\mu\left(\mathbf{e}_r+\mathbf{e}\right)=\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{C} = \dot{\mathbf{r}} \times(\mathbf{r} \times \dot{\mathbf{r}})=v^2\, \mathbf{r}-r \dot{r}\, \dot{\mathbf{r}} .\]

Since \(\mathbf{C}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{e}_r\) and \(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{C}\), taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{C}\) gives \(\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{C}=0\): the vector \(\mathbf{e}\) lies in the plane of the motion.

The conserved vector \(\mathbf{e}\) is the eccentricity vector, a rescaling of the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector.

Kepler’s first law

Now take the dot product of the last equation with \(\mathbf{r}\). On the right, \((\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{C}\cdot(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{v}) = C^2\). On the left, writing \(\theta\) for the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{e}\), we get \(\mu(r + e\, r\cos\theta)\). Hence

\[r = \frac{C^2/\mu}{1 + e\cos\theta},\]

which is exactly the polar equation of a conic with a focus at the origin, semi-latus rectum \(p = C^2/\mu\) and eccentricity \(e = \lvert\mathbf{e}\rvert\). Bound orbits (\(e<1\)) are ellipses: this is Kepler’s first law. The eccentricity vector points from the focus towards the point of closest approach.

The second and third laws are derived in my post on Kepler’s third law.

A hidden symmetry

By Noether’s theorem, a conserved quantity signals a symmetry, but for the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector the symmetry is hidden. For bound orbits, the Kepler problem is mathematically equivalent to free motion on the surface of a four-dimensional (hyper)sphere, so it is symmetric under rotations in four dimensions, a larger symmetry group than the obvious rotations of three-dimensional space.

Progress

The project is proving more demanding than I expected, and working through the literature in detail takes time, but writing up each topic here is a good way to organise my understanding.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna. The remark about the four-dimensional sphere is based on Wikipedia.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. Nothing in the results, but the bound \(r \le 2a\) was stated without its derivation, and the derivation of the eccentricity vector stopped before reaching the orbit equation.

What changed. Both are now complete, with \(\mu = GM\) throughout.
entry.summary: Polar equations of the ellipse, bound orbits from negative energy, and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, which gives Kepler's first law.

entry.title: Symplectic Integrators
entry.content:
Summer research 2024: the three-body problem · Part 2 of 11

A weekly research log from my summer project at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

← Plotting and Visualising the Three-Body Problem  ·  Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem →

This post explains what makes an integrator symplectic, and compares second-, third- and fourth-order symplectic schemes on the figure-eight orbit.

What is a symplectic integrator?

Start from Liouville’s theorem in Hamiltonian mechanics: the flow of a Hamiltonian system preserves phase-space volume. For one degree of freedom, a small region of the \((x, p)\) plane keeps the same area as it evolves, \(dA = dA'\):

So evolving Newton’s equations forward by a finite time defines an area-preserving (more generally, symplectic) map of phase space. A symplectic integrator is a numerical method whose single step is itself a symplectic map.

This matters for long simulations. A symplectic integrator does not conserve the energy exactly, but it exactly conserves a slightly modified “shadow” Hamiltonian, so the energy error stays bounded and oscillates instead of drifting. Non-symplectic methods such as the explicit Euler method and RK4 show a steady energy drift.

Checking whether a scheme is symplectic

For one degree of freedom, write a step of a linear scheme as

\[\begin{pmatrix} x_{n+1} \\ p_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=A\begin{pmatrix} x_n \\ p_n \end{pmatrix}.\]

The scheme is symplectic if and only if \(\det A = 1\). For a nonlinear scheme the same test is applied to the Jacobian of the map, and in higher dimensions the condition becomes \(M^{T}JM = J\) for the Jacobian \(M\) and the standard symplectic matrix \(J\).

Higher-order schemes

A family of explicit symplectic schemes applies, for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) within each time step \(\Delta t\), the updates

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}_{i+1}&=\mathbf{v}_i+d_i\, \mathbf{a}\left(\mathbf{x}_i\right) \Delta t, \\ \mathbf{x}_{i+1}&=\mathbf{x}_i+c_i\, \mathbf{v}_{i+1}\, \Delta t, \end{aligned}\]

with suitably chosen coefficients. A third-order scheme (Ruth) uses

\[c = \left(1, -\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right), \qquad d = \left(-\tfrac{1}{24}, \tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{7}{24}\right),\]

and a fourth-order scheme (Forest–Ruth) uses

\[\begin{aligned} c &= \left(\frac{1}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})},\ \frac{1 - 2^{1/3}}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})},\ \frac{1 - 2^{1/3}}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})},\ \frac{1}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})}\right), \\ d &= \left(\frac{1}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ -\frac{2^{1/3}}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ \frac{1}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ 0\right). \end{aligned}\]

Each sub-step is a “kick” followed by a “drift”, both symplectic maps, so their composition is symplectic too.

Accuracy of the higher-order schemes

I integrated the figure-eight orbit for \(50\,000\) steps with \(\Delta t = 0.01\). The energy deviations were:

Scheme Order Energy deviation
Velocity Verlet 2 \(5.9 \times 10^{-5}\)
Ruth 3 \(4.1 \times 10^{-8}\)
Forest–Ruth 4 \(1.9 \times 10^{-8}\)

The higher-order schemes improve the energy conservation by more than three orders of magnitude.

A remaining problem: momentum

For pairwise forces like gravity, the total linear momentum should be conserved to round-off precision by all of these schemes. In my simulation it drifted: the error was small, but it grew steadily with time.

Gallery

The animations are a highlight of this project:

And an animation of a perturbed figure-eight:

Credits

The section on the definition of symplectic integrators, including the figure, is based on these notes on the leapfrog method by Peter Young.

Changes on 25 October 2026

What was wrong. Nothing in the results.

What changed. The definition of a symplectic map is given in general, the coefficients are laid out more clearly and the energy errors are rounded to two figures.
entry.summary: Why area-preserving (symplectic) integrators keep the energy error bounded, and how third- and fourth-order schemes improve on Verlet for the figure-eight orbit.
